title: The Deep Debt
premise: Paloma Brightwater, a peace-conference interpreter, built her life on being nobody: fluent in six languages, loyal to none. But a calendar invitation from her murdered handler summons her into an operation he planned in secret — the extraction of Dr. Ilan Voss, a defector carrying evidence that the peace talks are a laundering scheme for the very militias they were meant to disarm. As Paloma smuggles Voss through checkpoints and betrayals, she realizes he is bait in a trap meant to flush out her handler's network, and that her own buried identity is the final key. She survives by doing the one thing she swore never to do: stepping out of the shadows, testifying to the evidence at cost of her anonymity, and dismantling the conspiracy in open light — trading invisibility for justice.
about_author: Yara Okonkwo is a former conference interpreter who spent a decade working in conflict zones before turning to fiction. She writes thrillers about the people who translate other people's wars — and the moment they stop translating and start speaking.

chapters.title: The Go-Bag by the Door
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet her mid-assignment at the Meridian Peace Talks, interpreting a session she knows is doomed. She keeps her go-bag packed, her aliases current, and her past sealed. When her handler, Marek, misses their dead-drop check-in, unease creeps in. Beat: the polished surface of her controlled life shows its first hairline crack.

chapters.title: An Invitation from the Dead
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Marek's body is pulled from the canal, ruled an accident. That night, Paloma receives a calendar invite from his account for tomorrow at dawn: a location, a codeword, her name. She knows the dead don't send email. Torn between fleeing and honoring whatever Marek planned, she goes. Beat: grief curdling into dread and resolve.

chapters.title: The Dead Drop That Breathes
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the dawn meeting she finds not a person but a dead-drop cache: Marek's contingency file, a burner, and a photograph of Dr. Ilan Voss — a defector inside the delegation's security detail with proof the talks launder militia money. The file names Paloma as the only extractor he trusted. Beat: the terrifying weight of being chosen.

chapters.title: Six Languages of Lying
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She approaches Voss through the conference itself, using an interpreting session as cover to pass him Marek's codeword. Voss is paranoid, half-convinced she's the trap. Their cat-and-mouse negotiation reveals he suspects a mole inside Marek's own network — someone who speaks all her languages. Beat: wary alliance forged in mutual suspicion.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Serenade
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Paloma and Voss. The extraction begins: a night drive through three checkpoints using forged credentials and Paloma's flawless accents. It works until the third checkpoint, where a guard addresses her by a name she abandoned fifteen years ago. Beat: her buried past reaching out to touch her — panic, then cold clarity.

chapters.title: The Name I Buried
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashback. The guard's recognition forces Paloma to confront her origin: she was once a witness-in-hiding whose testimony was buried when the peace process needed her silence. Voss realizes her identity is itself evidence — she's not just the courier, she's a living exhibit. Beat: the cost of survival reckoned; identity reclaimed as a weapon.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss confesses: Marek suspected the mole would use the extraction to surface, and Voss agreed to be the lure. The trap springs — a safehouse ambush by the mole's operatives, led by conference security chief Adeyemi, Marek's old friend. They escape through the flooded undercity, but the burner is compromised. Beat: betrayal confirmed; trust between Paloma and Voss forged in fire.

chapters.title: The Mole's Voice
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Analyzing intercepted transmissions, Paloma identifies the mole by a linguistic fingerprint — a regional idiom only one person at the talks would use: the chief mediator, Halvorsen, architect of the peace process itself. She realizes Marek died because he got too close, and the invitation was his posthumous checkmate. Beat: righteous fury; the enemy revealed as the face of peace.

chapters.title: Everything Louder Than a Whisper
chapters.summary: Paloma and Voss, split POV. Instead of running, they go loud: Paloma uses her interpreter credentials to access the closing plenary, and as Halvorsen delivers his triumphal address, she takes the interpreter's booth and translates his coded instructions to the militias live, in front of every delegation, while Voss streams the evidence. Beat: the climax — invisibility abandoned, her voice as the weapon.

chapters.title: The Interpreter Speaks for Herself
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In the aftermath, Halvorsen is arrested, the talks collapse into something honest, and Paloma gives testimony under her real name for the first time in fifteen years. Marek's file is closed; her go-bag stays by the door, but unpacked. She and Voss part as equals, survivors of the same war. Beat: resolution — the price of survival paid, and worth it.
